title: Electrolit vs Pedialyte: Which Is Better for Hangovers and Hydration?
excerpt: Electrolit vs Pedialyte compared: what's in each, which works better for a hangover, a stomach bug, or a sick child, sugar and taste differences, honest pros and cons, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Electrolit vs Pedialyte: what's in each, which is better for a hangover or stomach bug, sugar and taste differences, honest pros and cons.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Electrolit and Pedialyte are closer than most people think. Both are oral rehydration drinks, which means both are built around the same idea: some sodium, some potassium, and a small amount of sugar that helps your gut pull the salt and water in. Neither is a sports drink, and neither is a hangover cure. For a rough morning after drinking, either one will rehydrate you about as well as the other. The real differences are taste, bottle size, price per serving, sugar content in particular versions, and where you can buy them. Pedialyte has the longer medical track record, especially for children. Electrolit tastes better to a lot of people and comes in a bigger bottle.

**The quick picks:**

- **For a sick child, or anyone with vomiting or diarrhea:** Pedialyte (or a store-brand pediatric oral rehydration solution), used as the label or your doctor directs.
- **For a hangover, if you can stomach the taste:** either one. Pick the one you'll actually finish.
- **If Pedialyte's taste makes you gag:** Electrolit is the most direct swap.
- **If you're watching sugar:** compare labels. Both brands sell lower-sugar or sugar-free versions in some markets, and the regular versions are already much lower in sugar than Gatorade.
- **If you just had two or three drinks and feel fine:** a couple of glasses of water and some food will usually do the job. You don't need either one.

> **When to see a doctor instead of reaching for a drink.** Electrolyte drinks are for mild dehydration. **Get medical care if** you can't keep any fluids down for several hours, you haven't urinated in 8 hours or more, you feel dizzy or faint when you stand, you're confused, you're vomiting blood or what looks like coffee grounds, or you have a fever with severe diarrhea. **Call 911 right away** if someone who has been drinking can't be woken up, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and no drink fixes that. If you drink heavily most days and get shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or see or hear things that aren't there within a day or two of stopping, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous. Tell a doctor or go to urgent care. For babies and young children who are vomiting or have diarrhea, call your pediatrician for advice on how much rehydration solution to give.

## What Electrolit and Pedialyte Actually Are

Both drinks are versions of something doctors call an **oral rehydration solution**, or ORS. In Mexico and much of Latin America, people simply call it **suero** (or *suero oral*), and keeping a bottle in the fridge for *la cruda* is about as normal as keeping aspirin in the medicine cabinet.

Oral rehydration solutions are one of the quiet success stories of modern medicine. In the 1960s and 70s, researchers worked out that sodium and glucose are absorbed together in the small intestine. When the two are present in the right balance, the gut pulls in water along with them, even when someone has severe diarrhea. The World Health Organization and UNICEF built a standard formula around this, and it has saved millions of lives from cholera and other diarrheal illness, mostly in children.

The key point for comparing brands is that **an ORS is not just salty water and not just sugar water.** It's a specific ratio. Too much sugar and the drink can actually pull water *into* the gut and make diarrhea worse. Too little sodium and it doesn't rehydrate much better than plain water. That's the line between an ORS like Pedialyte or Electrolit and a sports drink like Gatorade.

### Pedialyte

Pedialyte is made by Abbott, the large US healthcare company. It started as a product for children with vomiting and diarrhea, and pediatricians have recommended it for decades. Over the years Abbott has added lines aimed at adults, including versions with more electrolytes, powder sticks, freezer pops, and sugar-free versions sweetened with non-sugar sweeteners.

The classic ready-to-drink formula is close to what the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends for a maintenance rehydration solution. Per liter, Pedialyte Classic has about **45 mEq of sodium** (roughly 1,035 mg), about **20 mEq of potassium**, about 35 mEq of chloride, and about **25 grams of dextrose** (a form of glucose). In a 12-ounce glass, that works out to roughly 370 mg of sodium, 280 mg of potassium, and about 9 grams of sugar.

### Electrolit

Electrolit is made by a Mexican pharmaceutical group and has been sold in Mexico for years as a *suero*. It's now everywhere in US grocery, convenience, and big-box stores, usually in a tall bottle of about 21 fluid ounces (625 mL) and in a long list of flavors.

Electrolit is formulated as an oral rehydration drink rather than a sports drink. Its label lists sodium, potassium, chloride, calcium, magnesium, and glucose. The exact amounts depend on the flavor, the country it was made for, and the version (there have been reformulations over time), so the honest advice is to **read the Nutrition Facts panel on the bottle in your hand** rather than trust a number from a website, including this one. In general, its sodium sits in the same ORS range as Pedialyte, well above Gatorade, and its sugar is moderate.

## Electrolit vs Pedialyte: Side-by-Side

| | Pedialyte (Classic, ready-to-drink) | Electrolit (regular) |
|---|---|---|
| Type of drink | Oral rehydration solution | Oral rehydration solution |
| Maker | Abbott (US) | Mexican pharmaceutical group |
| Typical bottle | 1 liter (about 33.8 fl oz); also powders and pops | About 21 fl oz (625 mL) |
| Sodium | About 1,035 mg per liter (45 mEq/L) | ORS range; check the label for your flavor |
| Potassium | About 20 mEq per liter | Yes; check the label |
| Other minerals | Chloride, citrate (zinc in some lines) | Chloride, calcium, magnesium |
| Sugar | About 25 g per liter (dextrose) | Moderate glucose; check the label |
| Sugar-free option | Yes, in some lines | Lower-sugar versions sold in some markets |
| Taste | Many adults find it salty and medicinal | Many people find it sweeter and easier to drink |
| Long track record in children | Yes | Ask your pediatrician |
| Typical price | Similar per bottle; powders are cheaper per serving | Similar per bottle; bigger bottle |

For reference, the **World Health Organization's reduced-osmolarity ORS** (the medical gold standard for diarrhea) has about 75 mEq of sodium and 75 mmol of glucose per liter. Both Pedialyte Classic and Electrolit are a bit gentler than that on sodium. That's normal for retail products meant for mild dehydration and for people who are drinking them by choice rather than because they're seriously ill.

## Which Is Better for a Hangover?

For most hangovers, **it doesn't matter much.** Both drinks rehydrate efficiently, and the difference between them is smaller than the difference between either one and plain water. Pick based on what you'll actually drink.

Here's the part the marketing tends to skip: dehydration is only one piece of a hangover, and often not the biggest piece. Alcohol makes you pee more because it suppresses a hormone called vasopressin (also known as antidiuretic hormone), which normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. So you do lose fluid. But researchers who study hangovers have found that measures of dehydration and blood electrolyte levels don't line up well with how bad people actually feel. The headache, nausea, fatigue, and foggy thinking seem to have more to do with inflammation, poor sleep, low blood sugar, stomach irritation, and the effects of acetaldehyde (the toxic chemical your body makes as it breaks down alcohol).

So there is no good evidence that Electrolit or Pedialyte, or any electrolyte drink, cures or prevents a hangover. What they can do is:

- Replace fluid and salt faster than plain water when you've been throwing up or have diarrhea
- Settle a queasy stomach for some people, because small sips of a cold, lightly sweet drink go down easier than food
- Give you a little sugar if your blood sugar is low after a night of drinking on an empty stomach
- Help with the dry mouth, thirst, and lightheadedness that come from mild dehydration

If you had a few drinks and feel only a little rough, water, a real breakfast, and time will do most of the work. If you were sick in the night, have diarrhea, or can barely get out of bed, that's when an ORS earns its keep. For a broader look at the options, see our [electrolyte drinks for hangovers comparison](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared).

### Why taste matters more than you'd think

When you're hungover and nauseated, the best rehydration drink is the one you can keep sipping. A drink that's technically perfect but makes you gag is worse than a slightly less ideal one you finish. This is Electrolit's biggest advantage. A lot of people who can't stand Pedialyte's salty, medicinal taste find Electrolit easy to drink, especially cold.

On the other hand, Pedialyte comes in more formats. If you want to stock up, powder sticks are cheaper per serving and easy to store, and freezer pops can be easier on a very upset stomach than drinking anything.

### How to drink either one when you're hungover

- **Sip, don't chug.** If your stomach is upset, a few sips every few minutes is better than half a bottle at once. Chugging is a good way to bring it straight back up.
- **Drink it cold.** Both taste better cold, and cold drinks are often easier to tolerate when you're nauseated.
- **Don't drink a whole liter in five minutes.** Your body can only absorb so much at a time. Spread it over an hour or two.
- **Add food when you can.** Toast, crackers, rice, bananas, or soup give you carbohydrate and more salt. A brothy soup is a traditional *cruda* fix for good reason. Our guide to [traditional Mexican hangover remedies](/never-hungover/traditional-mexican-hangover-remedies-vs-modern-supplements) covers menudo, caldos, and other options.
- **One bottle is usually enough.** For a typical hangover in a healthy adult, a bottle of either plus water and food for the rest of the day is plenty. More isn't better.

## Electrolit vs Pedialyte for Vomiting, Diarrhea, and Stomach Bugs

This is where the choice matters more, because real dehydration from illness can become serious.

For **adults** with a stomach bug, both drinks are reasonable choices for mild to moderate dehydration. The ORS principle is the same. Sip small amounts often. If you can't keep anything down, or you're getting dizzy, confused, or not urinating, get medical care rather than trying harder with the bottle.

For **babies and young children**, Pedialyte has the advantage of a long track record. It has been used and recommended by pediatricians for decades, its classic formula follows pediatric guidelines, and there are clear dosing instructions for kids. If your child is sick, call your pediatrician, who can tell you which product to use and how much to give based on age and weight. Don't assume an adult-marketed drink is right for a small child, and never give a baby a sports drink, juice, or soda in place of a rehydration solution.

For **anyone with diarrhea**, avoid high-sugar drinks like regular soda, juice, or full-sugar sports drinks as your main fluid. Their sugar load can draw water into the gut and make diarrhea worse. This is one of the main reasons an ORS like Electrolit or Pedialyte is a better choice than Gatorade when you're actually sick. Our [Pedialyte vs Gatorade guide](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover) goes deeper on that difference.

## Electrolit vs Pedialyte for Sports and Heat

Both are sometimes used by people working outside in the heat, running long distances, or recovering from a hot day. Both can work. Keep in mind:

- They have **less sugar than a sports drink**, which is good for rehydration but means less fuel for long, hard exercise. Endurance athletes often need more carbohydrate than either provides.
- Heavy sweaters can lose a lot of sodium. If you sweat heavily for hours, you may need more salt than one bottle gives you. A sports dietitian can help you work out your own needs.
- For everyday workouts under an hour, water is usually enough.

## Sugar, Sweeteners, and Calories

Sugar is a common reason people compare these two. A few points to keep in mind:

- **The sugar in an ORS has a job.** It's not there only for taste. Glucose is what helps the gut absorb sodium and water efficiently. That's why the regular versions of both drinks contain some.
- **Both are much lower in sugar than Gatorade or soda.** Regular Gatorade has around 21 grams of sugar in 12 ounces. Pedialyte Classic has about 9 grams in the same amount.
- **Sugar-free versions trade some absorption efficiency for fewer calories.** They still provide salt and water, which helps, but without glucose they're a bit less effective as a rehydration drink. For a mild hangover that's a minor point. For real illness, the regular version is usually the better choice.
- **If you have diabetes,** talk to your doctor about which rehydration drink to use when you're sick, and how to count its carbohydrate.

## Who Should Be Careful With Either Drink

Electrolyte drinks are safe for most healthy people in normal amounts, but a few groups should check with a doctor first:

- People with **kidney disease**, because the kidneys handle sodium and potassium
- People with **heart failure** or **high blood pressure** who have been told to limit salt or fluids
- People taking medicines that raise potassium, such as some blood pressure drugs (ACE inhibitors, ARBs) or potassium-sparing diuretics
- Anyone told by a doctor to follow a low-sodium or fluid-restricted diet

For everyone else, the main risk is simply drinking a lot of them every day when you don't need them. That's a lot of extra salt and some extra sugar for no benefit.

## Price and Where to Buy

Prices change and vary a lot by store, so check locally. In general:

- **Per bottle**, the two are often in a similar range, with Electrolit's bottle a little larger than a single serving of most drinks and Pedialyte's liter bottle larger still.
- **Per serving**, Pedialyte powder sticks are usually the cheapest way to buy an ORS. Store-brand pediatric rehydration solutions are often cheaper still and have very similar formulas.
- **Availability:** Pedialyte is in nearly every US pharmacy and supermarket. Electrolit is now widely sold in the US, and it's especially easy to find in Mexico, Texas, California, and in Latin grocery stores and convenience stores.

If you're traveling in Mexico, Electrolit and other *sueros* are sold in almost every pharmacy (*farmacia*) and corner store, so there's no need to pack Pedialyte from home. Our [Mexico travel hangover guide](/never-hungover/ultimate-mexico-travel-hangover-prevention-guide-2025) has more practical tips for a trip.

## Honest Pros and Cons

### Electrolit pros and cons

**Pros:**

- Real ORS-style formula, much closer to Pedialyte than to Gatorade
- Many people find it tastes noticeably better
- Large ready-to-drink bottle, nothing to mix
- Widely available in Mexico and, increasingly, across the US
- Includes calcium and magnesium in addition to sodium and potassium

**Cons:**

- Exact formula varies by flavor and market, so you need to read the label
- Heavy and bulky to carry or stockpile
- Fewer formats (no common powder version in most US stores)
- Less established track record for use in young children

### Pedialyte pros and cons

**Pros:**

- Decades of use, including for children, with clear dosing directions
- Classic formula follows pediatric rehydration guidelines
- Many formats: ready-to-drink, powder sticks, freezer pops, sugar-free versions
- Sold almost everywhere in the US
- Powders are cheap per serving and easy to store

**Cons:**

- Many adults find the taste salty and unpleasant
- The number of lines (Classic, AdvancedCare, Sport, sugar-free) can be confusing
- Some newer lines are marketed hard to adults for hangovers, which can oversell what any rehydration drink does

## What About Gatorade, Liquid IV, or Coconut Water?

If neither Electrolit nor Pedialyte is handy:

- **Gatorade** has less sodium and more sugar. It's fine for a mild hangover with no vomiting or diarrhea, especially if you also eat something salty. See our [Gatorade for hangovers guide](/never-hungover/gatorade-for-hangover).
- **Coconut water** is high in potassium but low in sodium, so it's not a true rehydration drink on its own. Our [coconut water for hangovers guide](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover) explains where it helps and where it falls short.
- **Water plus salty food** works for most mild hangovers. Broth, crackers, or a salty breakfast plus a few glasses of water covers a lot of the same ground.

Timing matters too. Some people prefer to drink electrolytes before bed or alongside alcohol rather than the next morning. We cover the trade-offs in [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking).

## A Better Plan Than Just Fixing the Morning

Rehydration drinks treat one symptom after the fact. If you find yourself buying Electrolit or Pedialyte most weekends, the most effective changes are the plain ones: drink less and more slowly, alternate each drink with a glass of water, eat a real meal before you start, and stop a few hours before bed so your sleep isn't wrecked. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also add a supplement. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and on the brain's response to alcohol. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so think of it as promising rather than proven. There is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers on its own, and it does nothing to replace fluids, so it isn't a substitute for water or an ORS. Some people take it alongside their usual habits. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medication, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

- Electrolit and Pedialyte are both oral rehydration solutions, built on the same sodium-plus-glucose principle. They're far closer to each other than either is to Gatorade.
- For a hangover, either works. Choose the one you'll actually drink. Many people find Electrolit tastes better.
- For a sick child, Pedialyte has the longer track record and clear pediatric dosing. Call your pediatrician for guidance.
- Neither one cures or prevents a hangover. They help with dehydration, which is only one part of how you feel.
- If you can't keep fluids down, stop urinating, get confused, or see signs of alcohol poisoning or withdrawal, get medical care rather than reaching for another bottle.

**Related reading:** [homemade electrolyte drink recipe](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink), [LMNT vs Liquid I.V.](/never-hungover/lmnt-vs-liquid-iv).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Electrolit the same as Pedialyte?**

No, but they're similar. Both are oral rehydration solutions that combine sodium, potassium, and a small amount of glucose to help your body absorb water. Pedialyte is made by Abbott in the US and has a long history of use in children. Electrolit is made in Mexico, comes in a larger bottle, and adds calcium and magnesium. Exact amounts differ by flavor and version, so compare the labels.

**Which is better for a hangover, Electrolit or Pedialyte?**

For most hangovers, they work about the same. Both rehydrate better than plain water or a sports drink when you've been vomiting or have diarrhea. The biggest practical difference is taste: many people find Electrolit easier to drink. Neither one cures a hangover, because dehydration is only one part of it.

**Is Electrolit good for kids?**

For babies and young children who are vomiting or have diarrhea, call your pediatrician. Pedialyte has decades of use in children and clear pediatric dosing directions. Don't assume a drink marketed to adults is right for a small child without checking the label and asking a doctor.

**Does Electrolit have more sugar than Pedialyte?**

It depends on the version and flavor, so compare the Nutrition Facts panels. Both regular versions contain a moderate amount of glucose because sugar helps the gut absorb sodium and water, and both are much lower in sugar than Gatorade or soda. Both brands sell lower-sugar or sugar-free versions in some markets.

**Can I drink Electrolit or Pedialyte every day?**

Healthy people can, but most don't need to. On a normal day, water and food give you the salt and fluid you need. Drinking a bottle or more every day adds a lot of extra sodium and some sugar. People with kidney disease, heart failure, or high blood pressure, or who take medicines that raise potassium, should ask a doctor first.

**What is suero?**

Suero (or suero oral) is the everyday Spanish word for an oral rehydration drink. In Mexico and much of Latin America, people keep suero on hand for stomach bugs, heat, and la cruda (a hangover). Electrolit is one of the best-known brands, but pharmacies there also sell other sueros and powder packets.

**Should I drink Electrolit before or after drinking alcohol?**

Either can help with fluid balance, but the bigger benefit usually comes the morning after if you were sick or feel dehydrated. Alternating alcohol with water during the night and eating beforehand matters more than any electrolyte drink. There is no good evidence that drinking an electrolyte drink before bed prevents a hangover.

**When should I see a doctor instead of drinking more electrolytes?**

Get medical care if you can't keep fluids down for several hours, haven't urinated in 8 hours or more, feel faint or confused, or are vomiting blood. Call 911 for signs of alcohol poisoning such as being hard to wake, slow or irregular breathing, seizures, or bluish, clammy skin. Shaking, sweating, or hallucinations a day or two after stopping heavy daily drinking can be alcohol withdrawal and need prompt medical attention.
